596 596 THE GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEW THE GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEW The Indian Ocean has hitherto been underdeveloped in fishery terms, but much recent work, including that of the International Indian Ocean Expedition, has demonstrated that the northwestern part of that ocean may be the most pro- ductive region in the world, as John C. Marr emphasizes. A short but delightful chapter by William F. Royce discusses, among other things, sport fishing and dif- ferences between objectives in various types of fishery control and maintenance. It is in this chapter that the term "search and destroy" is used to describe large- scale fishing operations at great distances from the operating country, which ac- cepts no responsibility for maintaining the resources. Royce describes the value of recreational fishing to the angler, pointing out that to many fishermen the catching of salmon is often of minor importance; and he considers the problem of the management of the Loch Ness monster, "which should be maintained for nonconsumptive uses." There is much more of great value in "World Fisheries Policy." William M. Terry asks why fisheries should be subsidized and gives some answers. J. A. Gul- land describes the problems of fisheries for the developing countries, including the general problem raised by the entry of new countries into already saturated fisheries. Peter A. Larkin, in "A Confidential Memorandum on Fisheries Sci- ence," explores the difficulties and hazards of making predictions in fisheries, in a tone that suggests that he has grown wary of government departments in which the image of science has been receding. Brian J. Rothschild, Dayton L. Alverson, G. J. Paulik, and G. L. Kesteven all discuss the methods used in fishery science, in particular the value of the systems approach. Altogether, this is a useful book and evidence of what must have been most satisfactory seminars. - M. J. DUNBAR THE MEDITERRANEAN and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II. By FERNAND BRAUDEL. 2 vols.; 1,375 pp.; maps, diagrs., ills., bibliogr., in- dexes. Harper & Row, Publishers, New York, Evanston, and elsewhere, 1972-1973. $35.00. 94 x 5 3/4 inches. In 1949 Fernand Braudel's "La mediterranee et le monde mediterraneen a l'epoque de Philippe II," a work that drew on almost a quarter of a century of study, was published. That it was a magisterial opus was immediately apparent, and its reception was enthusiastic. Between 1949 and the mid-196o's the author worked in archives and libraries from England to Poland and extensively revised his text from the material he gathered. It is from the new edition, published in 1966, that the English translation is taken. Braudel was strongly influenced by two great French scholars, Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre (to whom he dedicates the work) and by the group associated with the journal that bore (and continues to bear) their stamp, the Annales, economies, societes, civilisations. Bloch, the medievalist, and Febvre, the historian whose book, so useful to geographers, was translated into English as "A Geo- graphical Introduction to History" (Alfred Knopf, New York, 1925), turned away from the popular (then and now) attitude that historiography is a sort of society column of past hierarchs and viewed it as a record of men living with the land, affected both by the ancient heritage of societies and by the torments and changes that result from social and economic forces. GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEWS 597 Braudel acknowledges his debt to the geographers with whom he worked at the Sorbonne and expresses his thanks. One can see their influence, especially in the first half of Volume 1. According to Braudel, his "intention in the first part of this book was to explore, using the concept of geographical space, all the per- manent, slow-moving, or recurrent features of Mediterranean life." It is the work of an historian who is conscious of the geographical facts of climate, space, landforms, distance, and communications - "my homage to those timeless realities whose images recur throughout the whole book, from the first page to the last." Furthermore, he indicates the depth of his historical view by not having "hesitated to step outside the chronological limits of a study devoted in theory to the latter half of the sixteenth century" to use sources that extend back through the early medieval period and the classical period, into "protohistory," and into "geographical genetics." And what an admirable method of study he used: he worked first with manuscript sources, and only after he had formulated his con- clusions did he compare them with those expressed in published literature. His bibliography - especially of archival materials - is immense, and the longer section on printed sources reveals his turn of thought: it is made up of works in virtually all of the western European languages and indicates the greatest latitude of his curiosity. In Part 3 (Volume 2) Braudel starts a necessary task with some reluctance and apology: the treatment of political history. Traditional historiography - all too often the detailed description of a talus of sterile chunks and flakes broken from the mass of human accomplishment - must be considered, he feels; but he is never enthralled by the personal name, the battle, the date, the king, general, or admiral. In fact, his fundamental interest runs to the other end of the social scale: "The Mediterranean in the sixteenth century was overwhelmingly a world of peasants. . .. Peasants and crops, in other words food supplies and the size of the population, silently determined the destiny of the age." He recognizes the possible permanent effect of "events" and gives them attention. But he is no chronicler; his taste runs to the wide-angle and to interpretation, "the search for structure and category behind the event." He turns instinctively to geography, to economic history, and to broad social trends for clues to an understanding of men and events. And his imagination and his philosophical compulsion are ar- tesian: they bubble out over the surface, giving life not only to fundamental trends and forces but also to the ephemeral growths of history wherever, in his opinion, they might contribute to an understanding of the great movements and changes in human societies. Material on Turkey in the Mediterranean - a much misunderstood and mis- interpreted subject - seems to be stated wisely and probably brings some degree of correction to the obliquities of Western historiography. His attempt to im- prove the condition by using available translation is laudable. Any book is open to some criticism. Most of that which can be applied to this work might, I think, be freely admitted by the author. His generalizations are sweeping; some are wonderfully suggestive, some dubious, but all are stimula- ting. Among them are: his conclusions about the Jews of the sixteenth-century Spain and the reasons for their treatment; the background of baroque art, its growth and its spreading political and social influence; reversal in the direction of dominant traffic flow over the Pyrenees as a result of major changes in politi- All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms

598 THE GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEW cal and economic conditions; the tentative conclusion that wars between contrast- ing culture groups, such as Muslims and Christians, took place at times of economic depression, whereas wars between related culture groups came at times of prosperity; the effect of the geography of the Adriatic Sea on historical events; the effect of climates on societies; the biological exhaustion of the waters of the Mediterranean Sea; and his extrapolations with regard to populations and sources of energy in the early nineteenth century. Even though many of his generalizations will be rejected for cause, they are never shabby, always the thoughts of a persistently inquisitive scholar who occasionally is levitated by his own enthusiasm. Braudel's erudition becomes distracting at times. The extravagance of in- formation presented is made possible by his immense intellectual capital; but his great knowledge and fertile imagination often tempt him to wander from the mainstream of thought up tributary valleys. Or, to change the metaphor, when reading the book one often feels as might a listener to a virtuoso musical per- former who introduces too many cadenzas, all dazzling but which break the theme line. For some readers these "cadenzas" may accentuate certain qualities of the book. If so, they should not be deprecated; and in any case, they can stimulate further research. They do, however, make one consider wryly the author's claim that he is writing "structural history." Although Braudel speaks of writing "total history," he does not succeed, de- spite the gamut of his interests. How could he - or anyone? His bias is that of a materialist; and his search for practical, material effects militates against effec- tive consideration of the arts, sciences, religion, or the seemingly irrational tastes that have colored culture. Furthermore, the relatively brief section on prehistory is weak, for the large amount of information gained since his work was first pub- lished has hardly been touched. But adverse criticism is really niggling. Braudel has cut a glistening gem, its facets refracting light onto many heretofore obscure areas of history. His accom- plishment results from a happy conjunction of his personal talents and tastes with a newly emerging, still resilient method of historiography designed by Bloch, Febvre, and the group associated with the Annales. Added to those advan- tages is his gift of expression. He turns elegant sentences on his literary lathe, solid with meaning (except for occasional flights into the blue), smooth, rhyth- mic, and clear; and his translator has done well by him. - DAN STANISLAWSKI All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms
